title: Heart & the Mediastinum
summary: Map the mediastinal compartments, the pericardium, the internal heart and its coronary supply, and the nerves crossing the chest.

lessons.title: Mediastinal Compartments: Esophagus, Thoracic Aorta, Azygos System and Thoracic Duct

levels.kid:
Your chest has two lungs, one on each side. The space in the middle, between them, is called the **mediastinum**. It is like a busy hallway in the center of a house.

Lots of important tubes travel through this hallway:
- The **esophagus**, a food tube from your mouth to your stomach.
- The **aorta**, the biggest blood pipe, carrying blood away from your heart.
- The **azygos vein**, which collects used blood from your back and ribs.
- The **thoracic duct**, a thin tube carrying milky fluid called lymph back into your blood.

These tubes lie close together near your backbone, like pipes packed behind a wall. Surgeons learn exactly where each one sits so they can fix one without hurting the others.
levels.hs:
The **mediastinum** is the central compartment of the chest, between the two pleural cavities (the spaces holding the lungs). It runs from the top of the chest (the thoracic inlet) down to the diaphragm, and from the sternum in front to the vertebrae behind.

Anatomists divide it with an imaginary flat plane, the **transverse thoracic plane**, which passes from the **sternal angle** (the bump where the manubrium meets the sternal body) back to the disc between vertebrae T4 and T5.
- Above the plane is the **superior mediastinum**.
- Below it is the **inferior mediastinum**, split into **anterior** (in front of the heart), **middle** (the heart in its pericardium) and **posterior** (behind the heart).

The posterior mediastinum is a crowded corridor holding four key structures:
- **Esophagus**: muscular food tube, lying right behind the heart's left atrium.
- **Descending thoracic aorta**: the main artery heading to the abdomen, sending small branches to the ribs and esophagus.
- **Azygos system**: veins draining the back and chest wall into the superior vena cava.
- **Thoracic duct**: the body's largest lymphatic vessel.

Real example: because the esophagus touches the left atrium, doctors can pass an ultrasound probe down the throat (**transesophageal echocardiography**) to get very clear pictures of the heart from behind.
levels.college:
**Boundaries and divisions.** The mediastinum lies between the mediastinal pleurae, from the superior thoracic aperture to the diaphragm. The transverse thoracic plane (sternal angle to T4/T5 disc) separates superior from inferior. This plane marks several landmarks: the aortic arch begins and ends at this level, the trachea bifurcates near it, and the azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus to join the SVC.

**Esophagus.** It begins at C6 (cricopharyngeus) and enters the abdomen through the diaphragm at **T10**. It is narrowed at four points: the pharyngoesophageal junction, where the aortic arch crosses, where the left main bronchus crosses, and the esophageal hiatus. It deviates left in the lower thorax and lies anterior to the aorta near the diaphragm. Arterial supply is segmental: inferior thyroid, aortic esophageal branches and bronchial arteries, then the left gastric artery.

**Descending thoracic aorta.** It continues from the arch at T4, runs left of the vertebral bodies, and leaves through the **aortic hiatus at T12**. Branches include posterior intercostal arteries 3-11, the subcostal arteries, bronchial (usually two left), esophageal, pericardial and superior phrenic arteries.

**Azygos system.**
- **Azygos vein** (right): usually formed from the right ascending lumbar and subcostal veins. It ascends on the vertebrae and arches over the right root at T4 into the SVC.
- **Hemiazygos** (left, lower) and **accessory hemiazygos** (left, upper) cross the midline behind the aorta, roughly at T8-T9, to join the azygos.
- It links the SVC and IVC territories, so it acts as a collateral route when the vena cava is blocked.

**Thoracic duct.** It begins at the **cisterna chyli** (around L1-L2), passes through the aortic hiatus, and ascends between the aorta and azygos behind the esophagus. Around **T4-T6** it crosses to the left, then drains into the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins. It carries lymph from everything except the right upper quadrant of the body (head, neck, chest and arm on the right), which drains through the right lymphatic duct.
levels.phd:
**Compartment schemes.** The classical four-part scheme (superior, anterior, middle, posterior) comes from cadaveric anatomy. Radiology increasingly uses the **ITMIG** (International Thymic Malignancy Interest Group) CT-based three-compartment model:
- **Prevascular**: thymus, fat and nodes.
- **Visceral**: heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus and thoracic duct.
- **Paravertebral**: the spaces beside the spine and the sympathetic chain.

Notably, ITMIG places the esophagus and descending aorta in the visceral compartment. This makes the classical "posterior mediastinum" a different region from the ITMIG paravertebral compartment, a frequent source of confusion when classical and radiological texts are compared.

**Esophageal wall and drainage.** The upper third is skeletal muscle, the middle third mixed, and the lower third smooth muscle. There is no serosa; adventitia is the outer layer, which allows tumors to spread early. Venous drainage is divided: the upper and middle parts drain to the azygos and hemiazygos veins, while the lower part drains to the left gastric vein (portal system). This portosystemic junction is the substrate for **esophageal varices** in portal hypertension.

**Aortic segmental anatomy.** Posterior intercostal arteries feed dorsal branches that give spinal radicular arteries. The dominant feeder, the **artery of Adamkiewicz** (arteria radicularis magna), arises on the left in roughly 75% of people, usually between T9 and T12. Its anterior spinal contribution explains paraplegia after thoracoabdominal aortic repair.

**Azygos development and variation.** The azygos derives mainly from the right supracardinal vein. An **azygos lobe** (about 0.4-1% on imaging) forms when the arch fails to migrate over the lung apex, carrying a fold of parietal pleura (the azygos fissure). In **azygos continuation of the IVC**, the infrahepatic (suprarenal) IVC segment is absent and infrarenal blood returns via an enlarged azygos. This is often associated with heterotaxy and polysplenia.

**Thoracic duct variability.** The textbook single duct is present in only about half to two-thirds of people. Duplications, plexiform segments and right-sided terminations are common. Lymph flow is driven by intrinsic contraction of the lymphatic vessel wall, respiratory pressure changes and valves. Lymph from the intestines (chyle) is rich in chylomicrons, giving its milky appearance.
levels.expert:
**Clinical consequences of the corridor.**

- **Chylothorax.** Thoracic duct injury produces chyle in the pleural space. Effusion triglycerides above about 110 mg/dL, or the presence of chylomicrons, confirm it. Because the duct crosses from right to left near T5, injury below this level tends to cause right-sided effusions, and injury above it left-sided ones. Causes include esophagectomy, thoracic spine and aortic surgery, and lymphoma. Management escalates from dietary modification to ligation above the diaphragm between the aorta and azygos, or to interventional radiology **thoracic duct embolization** after intranodal lymphangiography. Dynamic contrast MR lymphangiography now maps leaks and anatomical variants before intervention.

- **Esophageal perforation and esophagectomy.** Spontaneous rupture (**Boerhaave syndrome**) classically tears the left posterolateral distal wall, causing mediastinitis. In Ivor Lewis or McKeown esophagectomy, surgeons ligate the azygos arch and frequently the thoracic duct. Because the esophagus has no serosa, the anastomosis depends heavily on technique.

- **Aortic pathology.** Endovascular repair (TEVAR) covers intercostal origins. Spinal cord ischemia risk rises with extensive coverage, prior abdominal aortic repair, or occlusion of the left subclavian artery (vertebral and collateral loss). This risk is reduced by preserving collateral beds, staging repair and draining cerebrospinal fluid to raise spinal perfusion pressure. Aberrant right subclavian arteries passing behind the esophagus can cause dysphagia lusoria.

- **Neurosurgical relevance.** Anterolateral thoracic spine approaches (transthoracic or thoracoscopic) mobilize segmental vessels and must respect the azygos on the right or the aorta on the left. Most surgeons approach mid-thoracic levels from the right to avoid the aorta and heart. Preoperative localization of the Adamkiewicz artery with CT or MR angiography guides which segmental vessels can be sacrificed safely.

**Pitfalls.** An enlarged azygos on CT may reflect IVC interruption, SVC obstruction or right heart failure rather than a lymph node. A dilated azygos node at the arch is a classic mimic. Distinguishing ITMIG compartments correctly narrows tumor differentials: thymic tumors are prevascular, while neurogenic tumors are paravertebral.

**Open questions.** Thoracic duct anatomy remains poorly predictable in individuals. The value of routine prophylactic duct ligation at esophagectomy, which may affect nutrition and immunity, is debated, with mixed trial evidence.

keyPoints: The mediastinum is the central chest space between the pleural cavities
The sternal angle to T4/T5 plane divides superior from inferior mediastinum
The esophagus passes the diaphragm at T10; the aorta and thoracic duct pass at T12
The azygos vein arches over the right lung root at T4 into the SVC
The thoracic duct starts at the cisterna chyli, crosses left near T5 and drains into the left venous angle
Lower esophageal veins link portal and systemic circulations, the basis of varices

test.q: The transverse thoracic plane runs from the sternal angle to which vertebral level?
test.explain: The plane passes from the sternal angle to the T4/T5 intervertebral disc. It separates the superior from the inferior mediastinum.

test.q: Which subdivision of the inferior mediastinum contains the heart within its pericardium?
test.explain: The middle mediastinum is the heart in its pericardium. The posterior mediastinum lies behind it.

test.q: At what vertebral level does the esophagus pass through the diaphragm?
test.explain: The esophageal hiatus is at T10. The aortic hiatus, which also carries the thoracic duct, is at T12.

test.q: The azygos vein drains directly into which vessel?
test.explain: The azygos arches over the right lung root at T4 and empties into the superior vena cava.

test.q: Where does the thoracic duct usually terminate?
test.explain: It drains into the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins. The cisterna chyli is where the duct begins, not where it ends.

test.q: Transesophageal echocardiography gives clear images because the esophagus lies directly behind the:
test.explain: The esophagus lies directly behind the left atrium, so a probe placed in it views the heart from close behind.

test.q: Which vessels cross the midline behind the aorta to join the azygos vein?
test.explain: The hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins cross from left to right behind the aorta, roughly at T8-T9.

test.q: Which region drains lymph through the right lymphatic duct rather than the thoracic duct?
choices: Right head, neck, chest and arm
test.explain: The thoracic duct drains everything except the right upper quadrant of the body (right head, neck, chest and arm).

test.q: Esophageal varices form where lower esophageal veins connect to which system?
test.explain: The lower esophagus drains to the left gastric vein, part of the portal system. Portal hypertension enlarges these portosystemic connections into varices.

test.q: The thoracic duct begins in the abdomen at a sac called the cisterna ___.
test.explain: The cisterna chyli, around L1-L2, collects lymph, including chyle from the gut.

test.q: Name the bony bump where the manubrium meets the sternal body, used to mark the superior mediastinum's lower limit.
test.explain: The sternal angle (angle of Louis) is level with the T4/T5 disc.

test.q: The descending thoracic aorta leaves the thorax through the aortic hiatus at vertebral level T___.
test.explain: The aortic hiatus is at T12, and the thoracic duct passes through it alongside the aorta.

kidTest.q: Where is the mediastinum?
choices: At the top of the head
In the middle of the chest
kidTest.explain: It is the middle space of the chest, between the two lungs.

kidTest.q: What does the esophagus carry?
kidTest.explain: The esophagus is the food tube from the mouth to the stomach.

kidTest.q: What is the aorta?
choices: A small vein in the arm
kidTest.explain: The aorta is the largest artery, carrying blood away from the heart.

kidTest.q: What fluid does the thoracic duct carry?
kidTest.explain: The thoracic duct carries lymph back into the blood.

kidTest.q: The space between the lungs is like a busy h _ _ _ _ _ _ in a house.
kidTest.explain: The lesson compares the mediastinum to a busy hallway full of tubes.

advancedTest.q: A patient develops a right-sided chylothorax after surgery. Where was the thoracic duct most likely injured?
choices: In the neck near the left venous angle
Within the left supraclavicular lymph nodes
Below the T5 crossing, in the lower chest
Above the T5 crossing, in the left upper chest
advancedTest.explain: The duct runs on the right below about T5 and crosses left above it. A lower injury therefore tends to give a right-sided effusion.

advancedTest.q: CT shows a markedly enlarged azygos vein with no hepatic IVC segment in a patient with polysplenia. The best explanation is:
choices: An enlarged lymph node at the azygos arch
Azygos continuation of the inferior vena cava
Superior vena cava obstruction from a tumor
An azygos lobe from failed arch migration
advancedTest.explain: With the hepatic IVC absent, infrarenal blood returns via the azygos, which is associated with heterotaxy and polysplenia. An azygos lobe does not enlarge the vein.

advancedTest.q: Why does a neurosurgeon often approach the mid-thoracic spine from the right?
choices: The artery of Adamkiewicz arises mostly on the right
The thoracic duct sits mainly on the left side
The azygos vein is absent on the right side
The aorta lies on the left of the vertebral bodies
advancedTest.explain: The descending aorta runs on the left of the vertebrae, so a right approach avoids it and the heart. The Adamkiewicz artery usually arises on the left.

advancedTest.q: Under the ITMIG scheme, how does the esophagus's compartment compare with the classical scheme?
choices: It sits in the visceral rather than a posterior compartment
It falls in the paravertebral compartment with the nerves
It moves to the prevascular compartment with the thymus
It is split equally between two adjacent compartments
advancedTest.explain: ITMIG places the esophagus and descending aorta in the visceral compartment. The paravertebral compartment is therefore not equivalent to the classical posterior mediastinum.

lessons.title: Pericardium: Layers, Transverse and Oblique Sinuses

levels.kid:
Your heart lives inside a special bag called the **pericardium**. It is a bit like a pillow with a fist pushed into it. The fist is your heart, and the pillow wraps around it.

The outside of the bag is tough, like a backpack. It keeps the heart in place and stops it from getting too big.

Inside the bag there is a tiny bit of slippery liquid. It works like oil on a bike chain. Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day, and the liquid lets it slide smoothly without rubbing.

There are also two little tunnels and pockets tucked behind the heart. Surgeons know exactly where they are, so they can reach the big blood tubes during heart operations.
levels.hs:
The **pericardium** is the sac that surrounds the heart and the roots of its great vessels. It sits in the middle mediastinum, the central part of the chest.

It has two main parts:
- **Fibrous pericardium**: the tough outer layer. It is fused below to the central tendon of the **diaphragm** and blends above with the outer coats of the great vessels. Because it barely stretches, it stops the heart from overfilling.
- **Serous pericardium**: a thin, slippery membrane with two layers. The **parietal layer** lines the inside of the fibrous sac. The **visceral layer** (also called the **epicardium**) sticks to the heart's surface.

Between the parietal and visceral layers is the **pericardial cavity**, holding a thin film of fluid that lets the heart glide as it beats.

Where the serous layer folds around the great vessels, it leaves two spaces:
- The **transverse sinus**: a tunnel behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk, in front of the veins.
- The **oblique sinus**: a blind pocket behind the left atrium.

Real example: in **cardiac tamponade**, blood or fluid builds up quickly inside the sac. The stiff fibrous layer can't stretch, so the fluid squeezes the heart and it can't fill properly. This is an emergency.
levels.college:
The pericardium is a fibroserous sac enclosing the heart and the proximal great vessels.

**Layers**
- **Fibrous pericardium**: dense collagenous connective tissue. It is attached inferiorly to the central tendon of the diaphragm and anteriorly to the sternum by the **sternopericardial ligaments**. Superiorly it blends with the adventitia of the great vessels. Its low compliance limits acute cardiac dilation.
- **Serous pericardium**: mesothelium. Its **parietal layer** lines the fibrous pericardium, and its **visceral layer (epicardium)** covers the myocardium. The two layers are continuous at the **reflections** around the great vessels.
- **Pericardial cavity**: a potential space normally holding roughly 15-50 mL of serous fluid.

**Reflections and sinuses**
The visceral pericardium is reflected around the great vessels in two tubular sleeves:
- an **arterial sleeve** enclosing the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk
- a **venous sleeve** enclosing the superior and inferior venae cavae and the four pulmonary veins

The gap between these sleeves forms the **transverse pericardial sinus**. It lies posterior to the aorta and pulmonary trunk and anterior to the SVC and the atria. The venous reflection is J-shaped (an inverted U) around the pulmonary veins and IVC. This shape creates the **oblique pericardial sinus**, a cul-de-sac posterior to the left atrium that is closed above.

**Nerves and blood supply**
- The fibrous and parietal layers are supplied by the **phrenic nerves** (C3-C5). This is why pericarditis pain may be referred to the shoulder.
- The visceral layer is innervated by autonomic fibers and is relatively insensitive to pain.
- Arterial supply comes largely from the **pericardiacophrenic artery**, a branch of the internal thoracic artery.

**Clinical anchors**
- **Pericarditis** can produce a friction rub, and pain that eases when the patient sits forward.
- **Tamponade**: rapid fluid accumulation impairs ventricular filling. The classic signs are **Beck's triad**: hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds.
levels.phd:
**Developmental origin.** The serous pericardium arises from the coelomic lining surrounding the primitive heart tube. During cardiac looping the arterial pole and venous pole are brought close together. The dorsal mesocardium, which originally suspended the tube, breaks down. Its disappearance leaves a passage between the outflow and inflow reflections: this passage is the transverse sinus. The fibrous pericardium derives from the **pleuropericardial membranes**, which carry the phrenic nerves as they separate the pericardial cavity from the pleural cavities. This explains the phrenic course along the lateral fibrous pericardium.

**Topography of the sinuses.** The transverse sinus is bounded:
- anteriorly by the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk
- posteriorly by the SVC, the roof of the left atrium and the right pulmonary artery

On each side it opens into the general pericardial cavity. The oblique sinus sits between the reflections around the right pulmonary veins and IVC on one side and the left pulmonary veins on the other. It is roofed by the reflection between the superior pulmonary veins. Posteriorly it is separated from the esophagus only by the parietal pericardium and fibrous tissue. That relationship is why transesophageal echocardiography gives such clear views of the left atrium. CT and MRI also describe **pericardial recesses**, such as the superior aortic recess, which extends cranially from the transverse sinus along the ascending aorta. These can mimic lymphadenopathy or aortic dissection on imaging.

**Mechanics.** The fibrous pericardium has a J-shaped stress-strain curve. Once its reserve volume is exceeded, intrapericardial pressure rises steeply. The rate of accumulation matters more than the volume: a small, rapid hemopericardium can cause tamponade, whereas a slowly enlarging effusion lets the sac remodel and can become large before compromising filling. The sac also enforces **ventricular interdependence**, meaning the two ventricles compete for a fixed total volume. This is the basis of **pulsus paradoxus**: during inspiration, increased right-ventricular filling shifts the septum leftward and lowers left-ventricular stroke volume.

**Function debated.** Congenital absence of the pericardium, or pericardiectomy, is often well tolerated. This argues that the sac's role is supportive rather than essential. Proposed functions include:
- limiting acute dilation
- reducing friction
- acting as a barrier to infection
- anchoring the heart's position
levels.expert:
**Surgical use of the transverse sinus.** In cardiac surgery the surgeon passes a finger through the transverse sinus, behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk. This lets a ligature or cross-clamp isolate the arterial outflow before cardiopulmonary bypass. The same route is used to:
- separate the aorta from the pulmonary trunk
- place encircling devices for left atrial appendage exclusion
- deliver the left-sided lesions of surgical ablation for atrial fibrillation

The right pulmonary artery forms part of the sinus's posterior boundary. It is at risk if dissection strays.

**The oblique sinus in practice.** The oblique sinus is a reservoir for posterior collections. This matters after cardiac surgery: a **loculated** clot behind the left atrium can cause regional tamponade. Echocardiographic signs may be atypical, with isolated atrial compression and no classic swinging heart. Suspect it in a deteriorating postoperative patient even when the anterior pericardial space looks clear.

**Pericardiocentesis and drainage.** The traditional **subxiphoid** approach aims toward the left shoulder. Echo-guided techniques now commonly choose the site where the fluid lies closest to the skin, often apical or parasternal. Hazards include:
- the internal thoracic vessels parasternally
- the liver subxiphoid
- the coronary arteries in the epicardial fat

Recurrent effusions, particularly malignant ones, may need a **pericardial window**, made subxiphoid or thoracoscopically.

**Constriction vs restriction.** Chronically thickened, often calcified pericardium (after radiation, cardiac surgery or tuberculosis) produces **constrictive pericarditis**. Distinguishing it from restrictive cardiomyopathy relies on enhanced interventricular dependence, with discordant ventricular pressures across respiration on catheterization, and on preserved or increased tissue Doppler mitral annular velocities. Pericardial thickness alone is unreliable: constriction can occur with normal-thickness pericardium. Treatment is pericardiectomy.

**Recent advances and open questions.**
- Cardiac MRI shows late gadolinium enhancement of an inflamed pericardium. This helps identify **transient constriction**, which can resolve with anti-inflammatory therapy rather than surgery.
- Recurrent pericarditis driven by autoinflammatory, interleukin-1-mediated pathways is now treated with IL-1 blockade such as **rilonacept**, which reduced recurrences in the RHAPSODY trial.
- **Epicardial adipose tissue**, lying beneath the visceral layer, is being studied as a paracrine contributor to atrial fibrillation and coronary disease.

keyPoints: Fibrous pericardium: tough outer sac fused to the diaphragm's central tendon
Serous pericardium has parietal and visceral (epicardium) layers
Pericardial cavity holds a thin film of lubricating serous fluid
Transverse sinus lies behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk, in front of the SVC and atria
Oblique sinus is a blind pocket behind the left atrium, bounded by pulmonary vein reflections
Phrenic nerves supply the fibrous/parietal layers; tamponade gives Beck's triad

test.q: Which layer of the pericardium is also called the epicardium?
test.explain: The visceral layer of serous pericardium adheres to the heart surface and is the epicardium. The parietal layer lines the fibrous sac instead.

test.q: Inferiorly, the fibrous pericardium is fused to the:
test.explain: The fibrous pericardium blends with the central tendon of the diaphragm. It attaches to the sternum by the sternopericardial ligaments, not by fusion.

test.q: The transverse pericardial sinus lies directly posterior to the:
test.explain: The transverse sinus runs behind the arterial sleeve (ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk) and in front of the SVC and atria.

test.q: The oblique pericardial sinus is located behind which chamber?
test.explain: The oblique sinus is a cul-de-sac behind the left atrium, between the pulmonary vein reflections.

test.q: Pain from pericarditis may be referred to the shoulder because the parietal pericardium is supplied by the:
test.explain: The phrenic nerves (C3-C5) supply the fibrous and parietal pericardium. They share spinal segments with the shoulder skin, so pain is referred there.

test.q: Which set of findings forms Beck's triad in cardiac tamponade?
choices: Hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds
Cyanosis, clubbing, a loud heart murmur
Fever, friction rub, chest pain on lying flat
test.explain: Beck's triad is hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds. A friction rub belongs to pericarditis instead.

test.q: Why does a small but rapid bleed into the pericardium cause tamponade?
choices: The serous fluid clots and blocks the coronary arteries
The visceral layer detaches from the heart muscle
The phrenic nerve is compressed and stops breathing
The fibrous sac stretches very little over a short time
test.explain: The fibrous pericardium has low compliance, so pressure rises steeply with sudden volume. Slow effusions give the sac time to stretch.

test.q: The venous sleeve of serous pericardium encloses the venae cavae and the:
test.explain: The venous reflection surrounds the SVC, IVC and four pulmonary veins. The arterial sleeve encloses the aorta and pulmonary trunk.

test.q: The main arterial supply to the pericardium comes from which branch of the internal thoracic artery?
test.explain: The pericardiacophrenic artery runs with the phrenic nerve and supplies the pericardium. The musculophrenic artery supplies the diaphragm and lower chest wall.

test.q: The potential space between the parietal and visceral serous layers is the pericardial ___.
test.explain: The pericardial cavity holds a thin film of serous fluid that reduces friction.

test.q: Which pericardial sinus can a surgeon pass a finger through to clamp the aorta and pulmonary trunk?
test.explain: The transverse sinus is a tunnel behind the great arteries, so it lets surgeons isolate them.

test.q: The tough outer layer of the pericardium is the ___ pericardium.
test.explain: The fibrous pericardium is dense collagen that anchors the heart and limits sudden overfilling.

kidTest.q: What is the pericardium?
kidTest.explain: The pericardium is the sac that wraps the heart.

kidTest.q: What does the slippery liquid inside the bag do?
choices: It helps the heart slide smoothly
It feeds the heart with food
It makes the heart beat faster
kidTest.explain: Like oil on a bike chain, it stops rubbing as the heart beats.

kidTest.q: What is the tough outside of the bag like?
kidTest.explain: The outer layer is tough and keeps the heart in place.

kidTest.q: Who uses the little tunnels behind the heart?
kidTest.explain: Surgeons use them to reach the big blood tubes.

kidTest.q: The pericardium wraps around the h _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The pericardium is the heart's protective bag.

advancedTest.q: Embryologically, the transverse sinus forms mainly because:
choices: The septum transversum splits the cavity into two separate compartments
The pleuropericardial membranes fold inward around the pulmonary veins
The sinus venosus is absorbed into the wall of the right atrium
The dorsal mesocardium breaks down between the inflow and outflow poles
advancedTest.explain: As the heart tube loops, the dorsal mesocardium disappears, leaving a passage between the arterial and venous reflections. The pleuropericardial membranes form the fibrous pericardium instead.

advancedTest.q: A deteriorating patient after cardiac surgery has a clear anterior pericardial space on echo but isolated atrial compression. The most likely explanation is:
choices: A large slowly enlarging effusion that has stretched the fibrous layer
Congenital absence of the pericardium allowing the heart to herniate
A loculated posterior clot in the region of the oblique sinus
Constrictive pericarditis from long-standing calcification of the sac
advancedTest.explain: Posterior loculated collections behind the left atrium cause regional tamponade with atypical echo signs. Constriction is chronic and would not present acutely after surgery.

advancedTest.q: Pulsus paradoxus in tamponade is best explained by:
choices: Loss of lubrication between the two serous layers
Ventricular interdependence within a fixed pericardial volume
Coronary compression that reduces blood flow on expiration
Phrenic nerve irritation altering the pattern of breathing
advancedTest.explain: On inspiration, increased right-ventricular filling shifts the septum left within the constrained sac, so left-ventricular output falls. Lubrication and phrenic irritation do not change stroke volume this way.

advancedTest.q: Why is pericardial thickness alone unreliable for diagnosing constrictive pericarditis?
choices: Thickness tends to fall as constriction progresses over time
Thickening points instead toward restrictive cardiomyopathy
Constriction can occur with normal pericardial thickness
MRI images the pericardium too poorly to be clinically useful
advancedTest.explain: Constriction may exist without thickening, so diagnosis relies on haemodynamic interdependence and Doppler findings. A thickened pericardium is suggestive but neither necessary nor sufficient.

lessons.title: Cardiac Chambers, Valves and the Fibrous Skeleton

levels.kid:
Your heart is a pump about the size of your fist. Inside, it has four rooms called **chambers**. The two top rooms are the **atria**. They collect blood coming in. The two bottom rooms are the **ventricles**. They squeeze hard to push blood out.

The right side sends blood to your lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side sends that fresh blood to your whole body, so its wall is thicker and stronger.

Between the rooms are **valves**. They work like one-way doors. They open to let blood through, then slam shut so it cannot flow backward. That shutting makes the "lub-dub" sound a doctor hears.

Holding the doors in place is a tough ring of gristle, like a sturdy door frame.
levels.hs:
The heart has four **chambers**. The **right atrium** receives oxygen-poor blood from the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae. The **right ventricle** pumps it into the pulmonary trunk toward the lungs. Oxygen-rich blood returns through four pulmonary veins to the **left atrium**, and the **left ventricle** pumps it into the aorta for the whole body. Because the left ventricle works against much higher pressure, its wall is about three times thicker than the right's.

Four **valves** keep blood moving one way:
- **Tricuspid valve**: right atrium to right ventricle (three cusps).
- **Pulmonary valve**: right ventricle to pulmonary trunk.
- **Mitral (bicuspid) valve**: left atrium to left ventricle (two cusps).
- **Aortic valve**: left ventricle to aorta.

The tricuspid and mitral are **atrioventricular (AV) valves**. Thin cords called **chordae tendineae** tie their cusps to **papillary muscles**, which stop the cusps flipping backward. The pulmonary and aortic valves are **semilunar valves** with three half-moon cusps and no cords.

The first heart sound ("lub") is the AV valves closing. The second ("dub") is the semilunar valves closing.

All four valves sit in a plate of dense connective tissue called the **fibrous skeleton**. A real example: in **mitral regurgitation**, a leaky mitral valve lets blood squirt back into the left atrium. A doctor hears this as a murmur.
levels.college:
**Right atrium.** It has a smooth posterior part, the sinus venarum, derived from the sinus venosus, and a rough anterior part lined by **pectinate muscles**. The two parts are divided by the **crista terminalis**, a ridge seen externally as the sulcus terminalis. Openings include the SVC, IVC (guarded by a rudimentary valve), and the coronary sinus. On the interatrial septum lies the **fossa ovalis**, the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale, rimmed by the limbus.

**Right ventricle.** It is crescent-shaped in cross-section and lined with **trabeculae carneae**. The **septomarginal trabecula (moderator band)** carries the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle. The smooth outflow tract, the **conus arteriosus (infundibulum)**, leads to the pulmonary valve. The **supraventricular crest** separates inflow from outflow.

**Left atrium.** It is mostly smooth-walled, with pectinate muscles confined to the **left auricle (appendage)**. It is the most posterior chamber and lies directly against the esophagus.

**Left ventricle.** Its wall is thick and its cavity is roughly circular in cross-section. It has fine trabeculae and two strong papillary muscles, anterolateral and posteromedial. The smooth **aortic vestibule** leads to the aortic valve. The interventricular septum is mostly muscular, with a small upper **membranous part**.

**Valve mechanics:**
- The AV valves open passively when atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure.
- During systole, the papillary muscles contract, tensing the chordae to prevent cusp prolapse.
- The semilunar cusps fill like pockets during diastole and seal at their nodules and lunules.
- The aortic sinuses (of Valsalva) behind the cusps give rise to the coronary arteries.

**Fibrous skeleton.** It consists of four fibrous rings (anuli fibrosi), linked by the right and left **fibrous trigones** and the membranous septum. It has four jobs:
- anchoring the valves and myocardium;
- keeping the valve openings open;
- providing attachment for the muscle;
- electrically insulating the atria from the ventricles, so impulses pass only through the **AV bundle (of His)**.
levels.phd:
The fibrous skeleton is best viewed as a three-dimensional scaffold rather than a flat plate. Its central element is the **right fibrous trigone (central fibrous body)**. Here the mitral, tricuspid and aortic anuli converge with the membranous septum, and the penetrating His bundle passes through it. The smaller left trigone joins the aortic and mitral anuli. Between the trigones runs the **aortic-mitral curtain (intervalvular fibrosa)**. This fibrous continuity links the left (left coronary) and non-coronary aortic cusps with the anterior mitral leaflet. It is the anatomical reason there is no muscular infundibulum on the left, unlike the right ventricle's muscular subpulmonary conus.

The "aortic annulus" is not a planar ring. The semilunar hinge lines form a crown-shaped structure that crosses the anatomic ventriculoarterial junction. Segments of ventricular myocardium therefore sit within the aortic sinuses, and fibrous interleaflet triangles extend down to the ventricular level. The **virtual basal ring**, joining the cusp nadirs, is what clinicians measure as the annulus.

The **membranous septum** is divided by the tricuspid septal leaflet hinge into atrioventricular and interventricular components. This explains why some defects cause left ventricle to right atrium (Gerbode-type) shunting. **Koch's triangle** contains the compact AV node at its apex. It is bounded by the **tendon of Todaro**, the septal tricuspid hinge, and the coronary sinus orifice.

The mitral valve is a complex apparatus: annulus, anterior and posterior leaflets (with Carpentier segments A1-A3 and P1-P3), chordae, papillary muscles, and the left ventricular wall. Its saddle-shaped annulus lowers leaflet stress, and flattening of this shape predicts repair failure. Chordae come in three orders: primary (free edge), secondary (rough zone, structural), and tertiary (basal).

The tricuspid annulus is larger, more dynamic and less supported by fibrous tissue, particularly along its anterior and posterior segments. This explains why functional tricuspid regurgitation follows annular dilation. The mitral annulus, by contrast, is partly anchored by the trigones.

Right ventricular inflow, apical trabecular and outflow components reflect separate developmental origins. The outflow tract derives from the second heart field. The **bicuspid aortic valve**, present in about 1-2% of people, usually reflects fusion of the right and left coronary cusps.
levels.expert:
Valve anatomy now drives catheter-based therapy, so detail at the trigone level has direct clinical weight.

**Conduction-system risk.** In transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), the His bundle runs just beneath the interleaflet triangle between the non-coronary and right coronary cusps. A short membranous septum and deep valve implantation predict new left bundle branch block and the need for a permanent pacemaker. Operators measure membranous septal length on CT and aim for higher implantation, or use cusp-overlap fluoroscopic views to protect it. Surgical aortic, tricuspid and VSD repairs all put sutures near the central fibrous body, which carries a similar risk of heart block.

**Measurement pitfalls.** Sizing the aortic annulus with 2D echocardiography underestimates its oval, crown-like geometry. Multidetector CT perimeter or area at the virtual basal ring is now standard. Undersizing risks paravalvular leak; oversizing risks annular rupture, especially with calcium in the left ventricular outflow tract. In bicuspid valves, raphe calcification and the frequently associated aortopathy complicate anchoring.

**Mitral interventions.** Edge-to-edge repair recreates the Alfieri double orifice. Success depends on leaflet length, tissue in the grasping zone and the absence of a cleft. Transcatheter mitral replacement is constrained by left ventricular outflow tract obstruction: the displaced anterior leaflet and the aortic-mitral angle form a "neo-LVOT," which is predicted on CT before the procedure. Mitral annular calcification, often next to the circumflex artery, makes surgery hazardous.

**Tricuspid.** Once called "the forgotten valve," it now has dedicated transcatheter repair and replacement devices. Leads from implanted cardiac devices crossing the valve are a recognized cause of regurgitation. The coronary sinus orifice and AV node lie close to repair sites.

**Left atrial appendage.** Its complex lobulation, described in the "chicken-wing" and other morphology types, influences clot risk in atrial fibrillation. It also determines suitability for occlusion devices.

**Open questions.**
- Annular dynamics in health versus functional regurgitation.
- The durability of transcatheter valves in younger patients.
- Whether fibrous trigone stiffness varies enough between people to matter for device design.
- 4D CT and patient-specific computational models, which are moving valve planning toward individualized anatomy.

keyPoints: Atria receive blood; ventricles pump it out, and the LV wall is about 3x thicker than the RV's
AV valves (tricuspid, mitral) use chordae tendineae and papillary muscles to prevent prolapse
Semilunar valves (pulmonary, aortic) have three pocket-like cusps and no chordae
The crista terminalis divides the smooth and trabeculated parts of the right atrium; the moderator band carries the right bundle branch
The fibrous skeleton anchors the valves and electrically insulates atria from ventricles, except at the His bundle
The central fibrous body and Koch's triangle locate the conduction system, a key risk in valve procedures

advancedTest.q: Why is new conduction block a recognized complication of TAVI?

The prosthesis compresses the sinoatrial node in the right atrium

A thicker trabecular layer that fills the outflow tract

The posterior leaflet seals the left atrial appendage
The device shortens the membranous septum

lessons.title: Coronary Arteries, Dominance and Cardiac Veins

levels.kid:
Your heart is a muscle that pumps blood to your whole body. But the heart muscle needs its own food and oxygen too! It gets them from special tubes wrapped around the outside of the heart, like a crown. These are called **coronary arteries**. "Corona" means crown.

There are two main ones, a left one and a right one. They start right at the beginning of the big pipe that leaves the heart. They branch like a tree to reach every part of the muscle.

If one of these tubes gets blocked, part of the heart muscle cannot get oxygen. That is a heart attack.

Used blood comes back through **cardiac veins**, which drain into the right side of the heart.
levels.hs:
The heart pumps blood to the body, but its own thick muscle (the **myocardium**) needs a private blood supply. This comes from the **coronary arteries**, which branch from the **aorta** just above the aortic valve, in small pouches called the **aortic sinuses**.

- The **right coronary artery (RCA)** runs in the groove between the right atrium and right ventricle. It mainly supplies the right side of the heart, and in most people the **SA node**, the heart's natural pacemaker.
- The **left coronary artery (LCA)** is short. It quickly splits into the **left anterior descending (LAD)** artery, which runs down the front of the heart between the ventricles, and the **circumflex** artery, which curves around to the back on the left.

**Dominance** describes which artery gives off the **posterior descending artery (PDA)**, the vessel running down the back of the heart. In about 70-80% of people it comes from the RCA, so they are "right dominant."

The coronary arteries fill mostly during **diastole**, when the heart relaxes. During contraction the squeezing muscle presses the vessels shut.

Used blood drains through **cardiac veins** into the **coronary sinus**, a large vein on the back of the heart that empties into the right atrium. A blocked LAD causes a large heart attack, sometimes nicknamed the "widowmaker."
levels.college:
**Origins.** The RCA arises from the right (anterior) aortic sinus and the LCA from the left (left posterior) aortic sinus. The non-coronary (posterior) sinus gives rise to no coronary artery. Because contracting myocardium compresses intramural vessels in systole, perfusion is greatest in **diastole**, especially in the left ventricle (LV).

**Right coronary artery.** It runs in the right atrioventricular (coronary) sulcus.
- **SA nodal branch**, from the RCA in about 60% of people
- **Right marginal branch**, along the acute margin
- **AV nodal branch**, at the crux of the heart, usually from the RCA (about 80%)
- **Posterior descending (posterior interventricular) artery**, in right-dominant hearts; it supplies the posterior third of the interventricular septum

**Left coronary artery.** The **left main** passes between the pulmonary trunk and the left auricle, then divides:
- The **LAD (anterior interventricular)** gives **diagonal** branches to the anterior LV wall and **septal perforators** to the anterior two-thirds of the septum. It also supplies the apex and much of the bundle branches.
- The **circumflex** runs in the left AV sulcus and gives **obtuse marginal** branches to the lateral LV.

**Dominance** is defined by the origin of the PDA. Hearts are right dominant in about 70-80%, left dominant (PDA from the circumflex) in about 5-10%, and **codominant** in the rest.

**Venous drainage.**
- The **great cardiac vein** runs with the LAD and then the circumflex.
- The **middle cardiac vein** runs with the PDA.
- The **small cardiac vein** runs with the right marginal artery.
- These veins join the **coronary sinus** in the posterior AV groove. The sinus opens into the right atrium, guarded by the **Thebesian valve**.
- **Anterior cardiac veins** drain directly into the right atrium.
- **Smallest cardiac (Thebesian) veins** open straight into the chambers.

**Clinical correlation.** Each artery maps to ECG territories: LAD to the anterior leads (V1-V4), circumflex to the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5-V6), and RCA to the inferior leads (II, III, aVF).
levels.phd:
Coronary arteries are **functional end arteries**. Anastomoses between territories exist, but they are usually too small at baseline to rescue tissue after sudden occlusion. Collaterals can enlarge through **arteriogenesis** during chronic stenosis. This growth is driven by raised shear stress and monocyte-derived signals, not by hypoxia-driven angiogenesis alone.

**Phasic flow.** Systolic compression of intramyocardial vessels is greatest in the **subendocardium**, where tissue pressure approaches LV cavity pressure. Left coronary flow is therefore mostly diastolic. Right coronary flow is more evenly spread across the cardiac cycle because RV pressure is low. Two things make the subendocardium the most vulnerable layer:
- Its perfusion depends on the diastolic pressure gradient (aortic diastolic pressure minus LV end-diastolic pressure) and on how long diastole lasts.
- Tachycardia shortens diastole and cuts its perfusion further.

This explains why ischemia is first subendocardial before it becomes transmural.

**Metabolic coupling.** At rest the myocardium extracts about 70-80% of arterial oxygen. Because extraction is already near maximal, increased demand must be met by more flow. Mediators of this **metabolic vasodilation** include:
- adenosine
- K-ATP channels
- nitric oxide
- hydrogen peroxide

Autoregulation keeps flow fairly constant across a range of perfusion pressures. **Coronary flow reserve** is the ratio of hyperemic flow to resting flow.

**Development.** Coronary vessels do not sprout out of the aorta. Endothelial progenitors arise from the **proepicardium**, the sinus venosus and the endocardium (lineage-tracing work by Red-Horse and colleagues). They form a subepicardial plexus that then invades the aortic wall to create the ostia. Disordered ostial connection explains anomalies such as:
- **ALCAPA** (anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery), in which flow later reverses and the myocardium suffers "coronary steal"
- interarterial courses between the aorta and the pulmonary trunk

**Dominance nuance.** Dominance describes the posterior septal supply, not the total myocardial mass perfused. The left system still perfuses most of the LV in almost everyone. Left dominance concentrates even more myocardium on the left main, which raises the stakes of left main disease.

**Conduction supply.** The AV node takes the dominant artery's crux branch. This explains AV block in inferior infarction, which is often transient because of vagal and adenosine effects and the node's dual supply via septal branches.
levels.expert:
**Imaging and nomenclature.** Interventional and CT reports use the AHA segmental model (proximal, mid and distal LAD and so on) and the SYNTAX score, which grades lesion complexity to help choose between PCI (stenting) and CABG (bypass surgery).
- **Ramus intermedius**: a trifurcation of the left main seen in roughly 15-30% of people. It is easily mistaken for a diagonal or obtuse marginal branch.
- **Myocardial bridging**: the LAD dives under a muscle band for a segment. It is common at autopsy and usually benign, but can cause ischemia, and stenting a bridged segment risks perforation or restenosis.
- **Anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery (AAOCA)**: an interarterial or intramural course is a recognised cause of sudden death in young athletes. Surgical unroofing is considered in high-risk anatomy.

**Physiology beyond angiography.** The appearance of a stenosis on an angiogram poorly predicts whether it is causing ischemia. Physiological indices measure that directly:
- **Fractional flow reserve (FFR)**: pressure across the stenosis measured during induced hyperemia.
- **iFR**: a resting, wave-free index that needs no hyperemia.

Trials using these indices (FAME, DEFINE-FLAIR, iFR-SWEDEHEART) support treating only the lesions shown to be ischemic. **INOCA/ANOCA** (ischemia or angina with non-obstructive coronaries) points to two other mechanisms: microvascular dysfunction and vasospasm. These are tested with acetylcholine provocation, and recognising them reshaped thinking about angina in women.

**Venous anatomy as access.** The coronary sinus is the route for **cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT)** leads, which are steered into lateral or posterolateral tributaries to pace the LV. Several anatomical features complicate this:
- The Thebesian valve can obstruct cannulation.
- The **Vieussens valve** sits where the great cardiac vein becomes the coronary sinus.
- Variable branching of the tributaries affects lead placement.
- The circumflex artery lies close to the mitral annulus near the coronary sinus, which matters for transcatheter mitral procedures.

The sinus also carries **retrograde cardioplegia** (heart-protecting solution) in surgery, but it perfuses the RV poorly because many RV veins bypass it.

**Grafting.** The left internal thoracic artery grafted to the LAD gives roughly 90% patency at 10 years and remains the benchmark. Saphenous vein grafts degrade by intimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis.

**Open questions.**
- Can collateral growth be therapeutically induced? Angiogenic gene and cell trials have been largely disappointing.
- Can the developmental programs above be reactivated to rebuild vessels after infarction?

keyPoints: RCA and LCA arise from the right and left aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve
Left main splits into the LAD (anterior septum, apex) and circumflex (lateral LV)
Dominance = which artery gives the posterior descending artery; ~70-80% right dominant
Left coronary flow is mainly diastolic; the subendocardium is most ischemia-prone
Great, middle and small cardiac veins drain into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium
Territories map to ECG leads: LAD anterior, circumflex lateral, RCA inferior

test.q: Where do the coronary arteries originate?
test.explain: Both coronary arteries arise from aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve. The pulmonary trunk carries deoxygenated blood.

test.q: Coronary dominance is defined by which artery gives rise to the:
test.explain: Dominance refers to the origin of the posterior descending (posterior interventricular) artery, not to the total myocardium supplied.

test.q: Approximately what share of people are right dominant?
test.explain: Most hearts are right dominant; left dominance is about 5-10% and codominance makes up the rest.

test.q: Which artery runs in the anterior interventricular groove?
test.explain: The LAD runs in the anterior interventricular groove. The circumflex runs in the left AV groove.

test.q: When does the left ventricle receive most of its coronary flow?
test.explain: Contracting muscle compresses intramyocardial vessels, so left coronary flow is mostly diastolic.

test.q: The coronary sinus empties into the:
test.explain: The coronary sinus drains most cardiac venous blood into the right atrium.

test.q: Which vein accompanies the posterior descending artery?
test.explain: The middle cardiac vein runs with the PDA; the great cardiac vein follows the LAD.

test.q: A blockage causing changes in leads II, III and aVF most often involves the:
test.explain: II, III and aVF are inferior leads, mapped to the RCA in most (right-dominant) hearts.

test.q: Which branches supply the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum?
test.explain: Septal perforators from the LAD supply the anterior two-thirds of the septum; diagonals supply the anterior LV wall.

test.q: Name the main LCA branch that curves around the left AV groove to the back of the heart.
test.explain: The circumflex runs in the left atrioventricular sulcus and gives obtuse marginal branches.

test.q: The natural pacemaker, the ___ node, is supplied by the RCA in about 60% of people.
test.explain: The SA nodal artery usually arises from the RCA, otherwise from the circumflex.

test.q: The heart muscle itself is called the ___.
test.explain: The myocardium is the thick muscular layer fed by the coronary arteries.

kidTest.q: What do coronary arteries do?
kidTest.explain: They bring oxygen-rich blood to the heart muscle itself.

kidTest.q: What does "corona" mean?
kidTest.explain: The arteries wrap the heart like a crown.

kidTest.q: How many main coronary arteries are there?
kidTest.explain: There is a left one and a right one.

kidTest.q: What happens if a coronary artery is blocked?
kidTest.explain: Part of the heart muscle loses oxygen, causing a heart attack.

kidTest.q: Used blood leaves the heart muscle through cardiac v _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Cardiac veins carry used blood back to the right side of the heart.

advancedTest.q: During tachycardia, which region is most at risk of ischemia, and why?
choices: Atria, because they receive the fewest coronary branches of any chamber
Subendocardium, because shorter diastole cuts its main perfusion time
Subepicardium, because its vessels are compressed most in systole
Right ventricle, because its coronary perfusion is mainly diastolic
advancedTest.explain: Subendocardial perfusion depends on diastolic time and gradient; tachycardia shortens diastole. Compression is greatest subendocardially, not subepicardially, and right coronary flow is spread more evenly across the cycle.

advancedTest.q: Why does a left-dominant circulation make left main disease more dangerous?
choices: Right coronary flow becomes mostly systolic in these hearts
The RCA then drains into the coronary sinus instead
The left main then supplies the posterior septum and AV node too
The LAD is absent in left-dominant hearts
advancedTest.explain: With the PDA arising from the circumflex, the left main carries an even greater share of myocardium, including the posterior septum and crux.

advancedTest.q: Why must increased myocardial oxygen demand be met mainly by increased flow?
choices: Coronary arteries lack smooth muscle to regulate their tone
Resting oxygen extraction is already near maximal, about 70-80%
Hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly in cardiac capillaries
Cardiac veins return blood directly into the chambers
advancedTest.explain: High resting extraction leaves little reserve, so demand is met through metabolic vasodilation and higher flow.

advancedTest.q: Retrograde cardioplegia through the coronary sinus protects the right ventricle poorly because:
choices: The Thebesian valve tightly seals the sinus opening
Right ventricular veins drain into the left atrium
Many RV veins drain directly into the right atrium
The coronary sinus drains mainly the left and right atria
advancedTest.explain: Anterior cardiac and smallest cardiac veins bypass the coronary sinus, so retrograde delivery reaches the RV unevenly. The Thebesian valve can hinder cannulation but does not seal the sinus.

lessons.title: Thoracic Nerves: Phrenic, Vagus, Recurrent Laryngeal and Sympathetic Trunk

levels.kid:
Your chest has wires running through it, like cables behind a TV. These wires are called **nerves**, and they carry messages between your brain and your body.

The **phrenic nerve** goes down to your breathing muscle, the diaphragm. It says "breathe in!" all day and night.

The **vagus nerve** is a long wanderer. It travels from your brain past your heart and down to your tummy. It helps calm your heart and helps your food move along.

A little branch of the vagus loops back up to your voice box. It helps you talk.

There is also a chain of nerve bumps beside your backbone. It is like a string of beads. It gets your body ready for action, like when you feel scared.
levels.hs:
Several important nerves pass through the **mediastinum**, the central chest compartment between the lungs.

- **Phrenic nerves** (left and right) come from spinal nerves **C3, C4 and C5** in the neck. They run down in front of the lung roots, alongside the pericardium (the sac around the heart), and supply the **diaphragm**. A saying helps you remember: "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive."
- **Vagus nerves** (cranial nerve X) leave the brainstem and pass behind the lung roots. They carry **parasympathetic** signals that slow the heart and stimulate digestion. Then they form a network around the esophagus and pass through the diaphragm with it.
- **Recurrent laryngeal nerves** branch off the vagus and loop back up to the larynx (voice box). The left one hooks under the arch of the aorta. The right one hooks under the right subclavian artery.
- **Sympathetic trunks** are chains of ganglia (clusters of nerve cell bodies) lying beside the vertebrae. They drive the "fight or flight" response, speeding up the heart.

Real example: a cancer near the aortic arch can press on the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient may develop a **hoarse voice**, sometimes before any other symptom.
levels.college:
**Phrenic nerve (C3–C5).** It forms on scalenus anterior, then enters the thorax between the subclavian artery and vein. It runs **anterior to the lung root**, between the fibrous pericardium and the mediastinal pleura, together with the pericardiacophrenic vessels.
- Right phrenic: runs along the SVC and right atrium. It passes through the caval opening (T8) or the central tendon nearby.
- Left phrenic: crosses the aortic arch and runs over the left ventricle. It pierces the muscular diaphragm on its own.
- Each phrenic nerve is motor to its hemidiaphragm. It also carries sensory fibres from the central diaphragm, the fibrous and parietal pericardium, and the mediastinal and diaphragmatic pleura. That is why pain from these areas is **referred to the shoulder tip**.

**Vagus nerve (CN X).** It descends **posterior to the lung root**.
- Right vagus: lies beside the trachea.
- Left vagus: crosses the aortic arch, lateral to it, deep to the left superior intercostal vein, which separates it from the left phrenic.
- Both give cardiac and pulmonary branches, then form the **esophageal plexus**.
- The plexus re-forms as the **anterior and posterior vagal trunks**, which pass through the esophageal hiatus (T10). The anterior trunk is mainly left vagal; the posterior is mainly right, reflecting gut rotation.

**Recurrent laryngeal nerves.**
- Left: hooks under the aortic arch, posterior to the **ligamentum arteriosum**.
- Right: hooks under the right subclavian artery.
- Both ascend in the tracheoesophageal groove. They supply all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid, plus mucosa below the vocal folds.

**Sympathetic trunk.** It has about 11–12 thoracic ganglia lying over the rib heads. They link to spinal nerves by white and grey **rami communicantes**.
- T1 often fuses with the inferior cervical ganglion to form the **stellate ganglion**.
- T1–T4/5 fibres feed the cardiac and pulmonary plexuses.
- Preganglionic fibres from T5–T12 bypass the ganglia to form the **greater (T5–9), lesser (T10–11) and least (T12) splanchnic nerves**. These go to abdominal prevertebral ganglia.
levels.phd:
The phrenic nerve's long route reflects embryology. The septum transversum, which forms the central diaphragm, begins at cervical levels and is innervated there. As the heart and lungs grow, it is displaced caudally and drags its nerve with it. The pleuroperitoneal folds and the body wall add muscle and peripheral sensory supply. Peripheral diaphragmatic pain therefore travels in lower intercostal nerves and refers to the abdominal wall, not the shoulder.

An **accessory phrenic nerve** occurs in roughly a quarter to a third of people. It usually arises from C5, often via the nerve to subclavius, and joins the main nerve in the root of the neck or the upper thorax. This explains why some injury patterns produce incomplete paralysis.

Recurrent laryngeal asymmetry follows the **pharyngeal arch arteries**. The nerves hook under the sixth-arch arteries.
- On the right, the distal sixth and the fifth arches regress. The nerve rises to the fourth-arch derivative, the proximal right subclavian artery.
- On the left, the sixth arch persists as the ductus arteriosus. The nerve stays hooked beneath it.

A **non-recurrent right inferior laryngeal nerve** occurs in roughly 0.5–1% of people, almost always with an aberrant retroesophageal right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria). Because nothing pulls the nerve down, it branches directly from the cervical vagus.

Cardiac innervation integrates both systems in the **cardiac plexus**, which lies around the tracheal bifurcation and aortic arch.
- Parasympathetic: postganglionic neurons sit in ganglionated plexuses within epicardial fat pads and act on muscarinic M2 receptors. Right vagal input preferentially affects the SA node; left input affects the AV node.
- Sympathetic: postganglionic fibres arise from cervical and upper thoracic ganglia and use noradrenaline at β1 receptors.
- Cardiac **visceral afferents** run with sympathetic fibres back to T1–T4/5. Convergence of these fibres with somatic afferents in the dorsal horn underlies referral of ischaemic pain to the chest and medial arm.

The esophageal plexus redistributes fibres so that each vagal trunk carries contributions from both sides. The anterior trunk gives hepatic branches and the anterior gastric nerve of Latarjet.

Open questions remain about the functional lateralisation and plasticity of the **intrinsic cardiac nervous system**, sometimes called the "little brain" of the heart.
levels.expert:
**Intraoperative and diagnostic pitfalls**
- **Left recurrent laryngeal nerve.** It is vulnerable during aortic arch surgery, ligation of a patent ductus, left upper lobectomy, and nodal dissection at the aortopulmonary window (station 5).
- **Ortner's (cardiovocal) syndrome.** Hoarseness from left RLN compression by an enlarged left atrium, pulmonary artery or aortic aneurysm is a classic sign. A new left vocal fold palsy warrants imaging from skull base to arch, not just the neck.
- **Unilateral RLN palsy.** It typically leaves a paramedian fold with a weak, breathy voice and aspiration risk. Bilateral palsy can cause airway-threatening stridor.

**Phrenic nerve injury**
- Cold injury during cardiac surgery, from topical slush, is a recognised cause.
- Catheter ablation is another: cryoballoon pulmonary vein isolation risks the **right phrenic nerve** near the right superior pulmonary vein and SVC. Operators pace the phrenic and monitor diaphragmatic contraction during ablation.
- Interscalene brachial plexus block very commonly produces transient ipsilateral hemidiaphragmatic paresis. This matters in patients with poor respiratory reserve.
- Diagnosis uses ultrasound or a fluoroscopic **sniff test**, which shows paradoxical upward motion of the paralysed hemidiaphragm.
- Treatments include diaphragmatic plication and, for high cervical cord injury, **diaphragm pacing**. Pacing requires an intact phrenic motor neuron and nerve, which is a key selection criterion.

**Sympathetic trunk interventions**
- **Thoracoscopic sympathectomy or sympathicotomy** treats primary palmar hyperhidrosis. Targeting the T3 (sometimes T4) level reduces the risk of **compensatory hyperhidrosis**, the most common long-term complaint.
- Dissection at or above the stellate ganglion risks **Horner syndrome**: ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.
- **Left cardiac sympathetic denervation** removes the lower half of the stellate ganglion plus T2–T4. It is established adjunctive therapy for refractory long-QT syndrome and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT).
- **Stellate ganglion block** is used as a bridging intervention in electrical storm.

**Vagal neuromodulation**
Vagus nerve stimulation is applied to the left cervical vagus for epilepsy and depression. The left side is chosen partly to limit effects on the SA node. Cardiac VNS trials for heart failure have produced mixed results.

**Open questions**
- **Ganglionated plexus ablation** for atrial fibrillation remains debated, because the efficacy and durability of autonomic modulation are uncertain.
- Mapping individual vagal fascicles, so that stimulation can be targeted to specific organs, is an active frontier in bioelectronic medicine.

keyPoints: Phrenic nerves (C3–C5) run anterior to the lung root and supply the diaphragm
Vagus nerves run posterior to the lung root and form the esophageal plexus
Left recurrent laryngeal hooks under the aortic arch; right under the subclavian artery
Diaphragmatic and pericardial irritation refers pain to the shoulder tip
Sympathetic trunk gives cardiac branches (T1–T4/5) and splanchnic nerves (T5–T12)
Left RLN palsy (hoarseness) can signal a mediastinal mass or aneurysm

test.q: Which spinal nerve roots form the phrenic nerve?
test.explain: "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive." C5–C7 contribute to the brachial plexus instead.

test.q: Relative to the lung root, the phrenic and vagus nerves lie:
test.explain: The phrenic nerve runs anterior to the lung root on the pericardium. The vagus passes posterior to the root.

test.q: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks beneath the:
test.explain: The left RLN loops under the aortic arch, behind the ligamentum arteriosum. It is the right RLN that hooks under the right subclavian artery.

test.q: A patient with pericarditis feels pain at the shoulder tip. Which nerve carries this pain?
test.explain: Phrenic sensory fibres from C3–C5 supply the pericardium. The pain is referred to the C4 dermatome over the shoulder.

test.q: Below the lung roots, the vagus nerves form a network around the:
test.explain: They form the esophageal plexus, which re-forms as the anterior and posterior vagal trunks.

test.q: Through which opening do the vagal trunks pass into the abdomen?
test.explain: The vagal trunks travel with the esophagus through the esophageal hiatus at T10.

test.q: Which laryngeal muscle is NOT supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve?
test.explain: Cricothyroid is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. The RLN supplies the other intrinsic muscles.

test.q: The greater splanchnic nerve arises from which sympathetic ganglia?
test.explain: Greater is T5–9, lesser is T10–11, and least is T12. T1–T4 fibres mainly feed the cardiac and pulmonary plexuses.

test.q: A tumour at the aortic arch causing hoarseness most likely compresses the:
test.explain: The left RLN loops around the arch, so arch lesions affect it. Hoarseness reflects vocal fold weakness.

test.q: The fused inferior cervical and first thoracic ganglion is called the ___ ganglion.
test.explain: The stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion lies near the neck of the first rib.

test.q: The vagus is which cranial nerve? (give the Roman numeral)
test.explain: The vagus is cranial nerve X and carries parasympathetic fibres to the heart, lungs and gut.

test.q: Branches connecting spinal nerves to the sympathetic ganglia are called rami ___.
test.explain: White and grey rami communicantes link the sympathetic trunk to the spinal nerves.

kidTest.q: Which muscle does the phrenic nerve control?
kidTest.explain: The phrenic nerve tells the diaphragm to move so you can breathe.

kidTest.q: The vagus nerve travels from the brain to the:
kidTest.explain: The vagus wanders down past the heart to the tummy.

kidTest.q: The branch that loops back up to the voice box helps you:
kidTest.explain: It helps control the voice box, so you can talk.

kidTest.q: The chain of nerve bumps beside the backbone gets you ready for:
kidTest.explain: It prepares your body for action, such as when you feel scared.

kidTest.q: Nerves carry messages, like wires or c _ _ _ _ _ s.
kidTest.explain: Nerves are like cables that carry messages between your brain and body.

advancedTest.q: Why does the right recurrent laryngeal nerve hook under the subclavian artery rather than a lower vessel?
choices: The septum transversum pulls the right nerve upward during descent
The right sixth and fifth arch arteries regress, so it rises to the fourth
The right ductus arteriosus persists and holds the nerve under the subclavian
The right vagus descends later in development than the left vagus does
advancedTest.explain: With the right sixth and fifth arches gone, the nerve rises to the fourth-arch derivative, the proximal subclavian. On the left the sixth arch persists as the ductus, which keeps the nerve low.

advancedTest.q: A non-recurrent right inferior laryngeal nerve should make a surgeon suspect:
choices: An accessory phrenic nerve arising from the C5 root
A retroesophageal aberrant right subclavian artery
A right-sided aortic arch with mirror-image branching
A persistent left superior vena cava draining to the sinus
advancedTest.explain: With arteria lusoria, no vessel drags the nerve down into the thorax. It therefore arises directly from the cervical vagus.

advancedTest.q: Irritation of the peripheral diaphragm refers pain to the abdominal wall rather than the shoulder because:
choices: Sympathetic splanchnic afferents carry its somatic pain fibres
Its sensory supply travels in the lower intercostal nerves
Vagal afferents from that area converge on lower thoracic segments
Phrenic fibres there project instead to lumbar dermatomes
advancedTest.explain: The peripheral diaphragm develops partly from the body wall and is supplied by lower intercostal nerves. The central part, from the septum transversum, uses the phrenic nerve (C3–C5).

advancedTest.q: Why is diaphragm pacing feasible for some high cervical cord injuries but not others?
choices: It depends on the stellate ganglion being preserved
It depends on the vagal trunks remaining intact
It requires intact phrenic motor neurons and nerves
It needs the esophageal hiatus to be anatomically normal
advancedTest.explain: Pacing stimulates the phrenic nerve. If the C3–C5 motor neurons or the nerve itself are destroyed, stimulation cannot drive the diaphragm.
